p.src: First: The tradition of narrative began with Master Zuo, yet critics still fault him for fabrication—how much more so writers of unofficial tales! Yet when its purpose is to encourage virtue and punish vice, invention is no crime. The works of fiction appearing in profusion today mostly depart from the classics and rebel against the Way, and cannot serve as instruction. Now and then there are works that borrow a subject to expound a lesson, seeking to awaken their readers by portraying murder, robbery, lust, and deceit; but some are mere patchworks rather than complete books, while others fabricate embellishments unlike anything commonly known. Though they attract eyes eager for novelty, they truly grieve one with the decline of refined letters. How could they compare with the rectitude of this book? Worthies of old compared it to Ban Gu and Sima Qian; I would say that it advances upon Zuo Qiuming and nearly preserves the lingering intent of the Spring and Autumn Annals. It therefore fully deserves to be called a “tradition.”

p.src: First: Liangshan Marsh lies within Yanzhou Prefecture in Shandong. The gazetteer writes its name as “Luo” and calls it eight hundred li across—an exaggeration. Yet men of old wished to drain the marsh and found nowhere to contain its waters, so it cannot have been small. The tale names neither Liangshan nor Song Jiang in its title: since this was no land belonging to rebels and Song Jiang was no man properly called a rebel, it is named only Water Margin. “Margin” means the water’s edge; the wording deliberately leaves the place unnamed. This makes clear that all beneath heaven are the sovereign’s subjects, and that Song Jiang dared not claim this marsh as his own. Does it perhaps express the thought of dwelling by the sea? How subtle was Luo’s choice of title!

p.src: First: Loyalty and righteousness are the virtues by which one serves one’s lord and treats one’s friends. A man without loyalty or righteousness is already rotten while still alive, and however fine his words, they will not be handed down. These one hundred and eight men are loyalty and righteousness gathered in the mountain wilds; these one hundred and twenty chapters are loyalty and righteousness made manifest in ink and brush. What is absent from the official histories, seek in the records of unofficial historians; what is absent among the robed and capped, seek among the common people. The intent is to stir men of virtue while denying petty men any pretext for pursuing selfish ends. Thus Master Li had good reason to restore the two words “Loyalty and Righteousness.”

p.src: First: A book values critical commentary because it can communicate the author’s intent and open the reader’s mind. When successful, it is like adding fur in the finishing touch or dotting a dragon’s eyes, bringing its whole spirit and splendor to light; when it fails, it is like slapping and smearing a face, defiling its original appearance. It must never be done carelessly. Here the purport of the whole work, the admonitory force of each chapter, and the spirit of every phrase and character have all been brought out, so that readers may know this is an unofficial history written with a historian’s brush, relevant to the moral order and beneficial to literary composition—utterly unlike the commercial editions of the past. Like following a musical score and striking every measure, or needling a bronze acupuncture figure and hitting every point, the commentator’s brush has a tongue and eyes, making all visible and audible. This is what is most precious in critical commentary.

p.src: First: This book portrays every circumstance and emotion to perfection and already paints life itself; is it not nearly superfluous to add actual illustrations? Even so, how many can perceive King Wen in a zither or Yao upon a wall? Thus the portraits on Cloud Terrace and in Lingyan Pavilion, and the pictures of the secluded and the displaced, can rouse and sadden viewers as though their subjects stood before them. Images therefore cannot simply be dispensed with. The present illustrations follow a new design rather than the old patterns: some are specially placed outside the chapter headings, others are selected in turn from within the chapters. Only the finest are chosen, for abundance is not prized.

p.src: First: Ancient editions contained Luo’s prefatory address and handed down such episodes as “Granny Lampwick,” but these can no longer be seen. Later men, however, made measured cuts because they felt constrained by the Four Great Outlaws, while others pruned the work because they disliked the prolixity of one hundred and twenty chapters. Both approaches were mistaken. The edition of Military Commissioner Guo is the old text; its relocation of the episode of Madam Yan is excellent. Yet its removal of Wang Qing and Tian Hu from among the outlaws and addition of the Liao realm remains merely a lesser writer’s method of making parts correspond. He did not understand that a master writer does nothing of the kind. In this book, for instance, Wang Jin opens the story but is never brought back to close his thread. This is why the work differs from all other novels and may indeed be called the sage of fiction!

p.src: First: The old edition removed the prolix tangle of poems and songs, fearing both that the thread of events would be broken and that the reader’s line of sight would be confused. It was admirably direct and lucid. Yet some verses portray human bearing and give modulation to the literary feeling, and these cannot all be removed. They have therefore been supplemented and revised anew: in some places the original has been altered to add what it possessed elsewhere; in others the intent of antiquity has been traced back and what was absent supplied. The sole aim is to encourage virtue and punish vice while also perfecting the humor, so that readers are moved and brought to a smile, without losing the profound, lingering savor that invites chanting and sighs.

p.src: First: The old edition also devoted considerable effort to correcting the text, pronunciations, and characters, yet many confusions, errors, discrepancies, and corruptions remained. The lyric quoted at the very beginning, for example, contains four errors at once. Compare the old edition against the present printing, and the rest will become clear. Cases such as writing “耐” for “奈” or “躁” for “燥” may still be called mere scribal errors. But “戴” is confused with “帶,” “煞” with “殺,” and “閂” with “拴”; “” and “衝” are left undifferentiated, as are “逕” and “竟,” so that the meaning itself goes awry. Examples of this kind are too numerous to enumerate; all have now been collated and corrected. Placing pronunciation glosses beneath the characters makes them easy to see, but their varying size and broken continuity offend learned readers. They have therefore been gathered at the end of each chapter for convenient reference. Distant recurrences are treated by analogy, while differing pronunciations are listed separately. Where even half the character permits it to be read, or the common meaning is intelligible, the gloss has sometimes been omitted.

p.src: First: Whoever sets forth a work must have some basis. This book fashions events from human feeling and originally need not seek corroboration in other books. Moreover, the names and numbers of the men recorded in the Mirror of the Song and Anecdotes of the Xuanhe Era can indeed be substantiated; the Classified Drafts from Seven Revisions likewise records their names and recounts Guanzhong’s thirty-six Heavenly Spirits and seventy-two Earthly Fiends. These two texts are now placed at the head of the volume, together with the native places and origins of all one hundred and eight men, for ease of reading and remembrance and to enrich conversation.

p.src: First: Those who record events extract their essentials, and those who compile sayings probe their profundities. Within the tale, Li Kui has already been singled out for a separate Biography of Shouzhang. Lu Da, , Wu Song, Shi Xiu, Zhang Shun, Li Jun, Yan Qing, and others could likewise each be made the subject of a separate biography, showing the whole course of their lives. As for its choice phrases and fine sentences, even its dialect, jests, and curses are enough to move the human heart. They are now specially brought forward to show that this book is filled with scattered gold that can never be gathered up entirely. Old Master Su Dongpo said, “The method of reading is to seek out a single meaning with each reading.” If even fiction possesses beauties such as these, how much more must the official histories!
